metadata.title: Micron Takes Unexpected Step as Tensions Rise

content.text:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.
Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) is offering Taiwan engineers roughly $32,000 in cash plus equity awards as the AI-driven memory boom produces record profits, but the unusually large compensation package also highlights a growing investor risk: retaining critical semiconductor talent while preventing a labor dispute from disrupting one of Micron's most important manufacturing hubs.
Micron is one of the world's largest memory-chip manufacturers, competing primarily with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The company produces DRAM, NAND flash and increasingly high-bandwidth memory, or HBM, used in AI accelerators and data centers. Surging AI infrastructure spending has dramatically strengthened memory pricing and Micron's earnings.
Micron plans to give Taiwan engineers a NT$1 million, or about $31,600, cash bonus along with equity awards. Entry-level engineers' average compensation for the past fiscal year will reach roughly NT$3.4 million after the awards, while all Taiwan employees will receive equity through annual merit grants.
The stakes are substantial. Micron employs about 15,000 people in Taiwan and has invested more than NT$1.6 trillion on the island. Reuters reported that unions representing roughly two-thirds of those workers are pushing for a different compensation structure, including allocating 15% of operating profit to employee bonuses, while another mediation round remains ahead.
That pressure comes during an extraordinary earnings cycle. Micron reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $41.46 billion, up from $9.30 billion a year earlier, and guided for roughly $50 billion of fourth-quarter revenue with an approximately 86% gross margin. HBM4 is already shipping in high volume for its lead customer.
Investors Takeaway
The immediate question is whether higher compensation becomes a manageable cost of protecting Micron's manufacturing capacity or develops into persistent margin pressure.
Investors should watch the next Taiwan mediation closely, particularly for signs of strike action or materially broader profit-sharing commitments. More importantly, Micron reports fiscal fourth-quarter results on September 30, when investors will be looking for confirmation of its $50 billion revenue target, 86% gross-margin outlook and continued HBM execution.
With DRAM and NAND supply expected to remain tight into 2027, maintaining skilled engineering capacity may be worth higher compensation. But labor disruption at a major production hub could become a much larger financial problem than the bonuses themselves.
